# **Rearchitecting OpenMMPA for Edge-First Android: A 4GB RAM Reference Architecture with LiteRT-LM, Firebase AI Logic, and JetBrains Koog**

## **Executive Architectural Synthesis: From Cross-Platform Flutter to Native Edge-First Android**

Migrating the Open-Multi-Modal-Personal-Assistant (OpenMMPA) from a cross-platform Flutter codebase to a native Kotlin Android application represents a fundamental shift from cloud-dependent middleware to a hardware-accelerated, local-first agentic architecture1. In its original implementation, OpenMMPA relied on Dart FFI bindings (objectbox\_flutter\_libs 4.0.3) for local storage and delegated speech and multimodal processing to external Firebase Cloud Functions (STTSFunctions), which required manual management of audio encodings (TTSEncodings.xlsx) and incurred round-trip network latency on every user interaction2.  
By targeting a native Android environment on a constrained 4GB RAM edge device, the rearchitected system eliminates the STTSFunctions backend entirely while unifying patterns from Google's reference implementations—specifically FriendlyMeals-Android for Firebase AI Logic, JetPacker (android/ai-samples) for multimodal itinerary and voice note workflows, and the Google AI Edge Gallery for local LiteRT-LM execution and Model Context Protocol (MCP) skill orchestration5.  
![][image1]  
A critical structural finding across Google's Android AI ecosystem is the deprecation of legacy inference abstractions. As of August 2026, the MediaPipe LLM Inference API (com.google.mediapipe.tasks.genai.llminference) is officially marked @Deprecated and placed in maintenance-only mode9. Furthermore, the legacy TensorFlow Lite Interpreter API has been superseded by the LiteRT V2 CompiledModel API (com.google.ai.edge.litert:litert:2.2.0), while generative language and multimodal embedding workloads have migrated to **LiteRT-LM** (com.google.ai.edge.litertlm:litertlm-android)3. Consequently, building a modern Android prototype requires bypassing deprecated MediaPipe GenAI wrappers in favor of LiteRT-LM and MLKit GenAI primitives, paired with JetBrains Koog (ai.koog:koog-agents:1.3.0), which includes a dedicated LiteRTLLMClient out of the box12.

## **Hardware Reality Check: The 4GB RAM Budget and LiteRT-LM Runtime Strategy**

Operating generative AI models on an edge Android device with 4GB of physical LPDDR4X/LPDDR5 RAM requires rigorous native memory accounting. On Android 12 and higher—the minimum OS baseline required by Google AI Edge Gallery8—the Linux kernel, SystemUI, Google Play Services, hardware graphics buffers (Gralloc/ION), and the Android Runtime (ART) zygote consume between 1.8 GB and 2.3 GB of resident memory before the target application launches. Consequently, the Android Low Memory Killer Daemon (lmkd) enforces an effective application ceiling of 1.1 GB to 1.4 GB of combined Java heap and native malloc/DMA-BUF memory.  
This hardware ceiling validates the hypothesis that **Gemini Nano** (backed by Gemma 4 E2B or Gemma 2 2B architectures via AICore and MLKit GenAI) is unsuitable as the primary resident model on a 4GB device. A 2-billion-parameter model quantized to 4-bit weights requires roughly 1.1 GB to 1.3 GB for static weights alone, and expands past 1.6 GB once the KV-cache, activation buffers, and XNNPACK/GPU delegates initialize—triggering immediate out-of-memory (OOM) termination when run alongside a vector database and an embedding model.  
![][image2]

### **Selecting and Configuring the Local Model Pair: Gemma 3 270M and EmbeddingGemma 2**

To stay comfortably within a \~650 MB native memory envelope, the architecture pairs **Gemma 3 270M** for text synthesis with **EmbeddingGemma 2** for semantic encoding19. Both models derive from the exact same Gemma 3 foundational architecture and share a unified SentencePiece tokenizer (tokenizer.model), which allows the Android application to load a single tokenizer binary into memory for both embedding and generation tasks22.  
Google DeepMind's **EmbeddingGemma 2** (google/embeddinggemma-2) is an open multimodal embedding model with 740M total parameters, mapping text, code, images, audio, and video into a unified 768-dimensional vector space across an 8K token context window22. Crucially, EmbeddingGemma 2 is constructed with a modular architecture comprising three distinct encoders: a 270M-parameter text encoder available standalone as litert-community/embeddinggemma-2-text-270m-litert-lm, a 170M-parameter vision encoder that processes image frames and visual scenes, and a 300M-parameter audio encoder that processes multi-language speech and acoustic events22. Because EmbeddingGemma 2 allows developers to toggle off or omit unused encoders at load time22, the application can dynamically manage its memory footprint on a 4GB device using LiteRT-LM's EmbeddingEngine API19.

| **litert-community/embeddinggemma-2-text-270m-litert-lm**23 | 270M (Text & Code only)22 | 4-bit / Mixed Precision .litertlm32 | \~175–190 MB32 | \~300–320 MB32 | **Always-Resident Default:** Co-resides in RAM alongside Gemma 3 270M for instant zero-latency query & document embedding19. |
| **litert-community/embeddinggemma-2-740m-litert-lm**37 | 740M Total (270M Text \+ 170M Vision \+ 300M Audio)22 | 4-bit .litertlm (GPU/NPU backend)19 | \~460–500 MB | \~680–750 MB (all encoders active) | **On-Demand / Modular Loading:** Omit audio/vision encoders during normal chat22, or instantiate EmbeddingEngine with vision\_backend=gpu during background media indexing when Gemma 3 270M is unloaded19. |
| **Gemma 3 270M (.litertlm)**17 | 270M (Instruction-tuned decoder)20 | 4-bit (int4) or Dynamic int8 .litertlm10 | \~180–260 MB | \~310–380 MB | **Resident Synthesis Engine:** Loaded via Koog's LiteRTLLMClient for offline RAG synthesis and local tool calling13. |

### **Critical Engineering Guardrails for EmbeddingGemma 2**

Implementing EmbeddingGemma 2 on Android requires strict adherence to three model-specific constraints discovered in its architectural specifications. First, developers must never configure the LiteRT GPU delegate or model weights to execute EmbeddingGemma 2 in float16 precision22. EmbeddingGemma 2's internal activation range exceeds the dynamic range of IEEE 754 float16, causing the model to silently emit degraded embeddings or NaN tensors without throwing a runtime exception22. When running unquantized subgraphs or activations, bfloat16 (which preserves the 8-bit exponent of float32), float32, or the official 4-bit and mixed-precision (e4\_a8\_f4\_p4) .litertlm builds must be used22.  
Second, because EmbeddingGemma 2 is trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) alongside Noise-Contrastive Estimation (NCE), a Global Orthogonal Regularizer (GOR), and Geometric Embedding Distillation22, its 768-dimensional output vector can be sliced by keeping only the leading ![][image3] dimensions and applying ![][image4] re-normalization22. On a 4GB device, truncating vectors to 256 dimensions—or 128 dimensions if the workload is strictly text-only—reduces ObjectBox HNSW graph RAM consumption by 66% to 83% with minimal retrieval quality degradation22.  
Third, EmbeddingGemma 2 relies on asymmetric, task-steered instruction prefixes prepended to text inputs—though never to raw image, audio, or video buffers—to steer representations into the optimal semantic subspace19. When indexing documents into ObjectBox, the text must be formatted manually as title: {title} \| text: {document}, whereas untitled documents use title: none \| text: {document}22. When embedding user queries or performing intent classification, task-specific prefixes for search, classification, or clustering must be prepended prior to invoking the EmbeddingEngine19.

## **Local Vector Storage: Migrating ObjectBox from Flutter to Native Kotlin**

In the original Flutter OpenMMPA repository, local persistence relied on objectbox 4.0.3 and objectbox\_flutter\_libs 4.0.32. A fundamental architectural clarification is required regarding how ObjectBox handles embeddings: **ObjectBox does not bundle an internal embedding model**21. ObjectBox is strictly a high-performance transactional NoSQL object store and Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexing engine; the host application is entirely responsible for transforming raw text, audio, or images into FloatArray vectors via an external model before insertion21.  
Migrating to native Android allows the application to upgrade to **ObjectBox Java/Kotlin/Android 5.4.1**26, eliminating Dart FFI serialization overhead and enabling direct zero-copy JNI buffer access from Kotlin coroutines. Furthermore, because EmbeddingGemma 2 uses a Global Orthogonal Regularizer (GOR) during training specifically to spread vectors uniformly across the embedding space, its representations are uniquely resilient to quantization and enable highly efficient ANN search in vector databases31.  
In Kotlin, defining the multimodal memory store requires annotating a FloatArray property with @HnswIndex24:

Kotlin  
package com.openmmpa.android.data.local

import io.objectbox.annotation.Entity  
import io.objectbox.annotation.HnswIndex  
import io.objectbox.annotation.Id  
import io.objectbox.annotation.Index  
import io.objectbox.annotation.VectorDistanceType

@Entity  
data class MemoryChunkEntity(  
    @Id var id: Long \= 0,  
    @Index var sourceUri: String \= "",  
    var title: String \= "none",  
    var contentText: String \= "",  
    var modalityType: String \= "TEXT", // TEXT, IMAGE, AUDIO, VIDEO  
    var timestampMillis: Long \= System.currentTimeMillis(),  
      
    // Truncated via Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) from 768d to 256d  
    // Using Cosine distance on L2-normalized EmbeddingGemma 2 vectors  
    @HnswIndex(  
        dimensions \= 256,  
        neighborsPerNode \= 16, // Reduced from default 30 to conserve RAM on 4GB device  
        distanceType \= VectorDistanceType.COSINE  
    )  
    var embedding: FloatArray? \= null  
)

Configuring neighborsPerNode \= 16 (the ![][image5] parameter in HNSW) inside @HnswIndex provides a critical memory optimization21. While ObjectBox defaults to neighborsPerNode \= 30, lowering ![][image5] to 16 reduces the in-memory navigational graph connectivity and resource usage on constrained mobile cores while maintaining high recall for personal assistant knowledge bases21.

## **Eliminating STTSFunctions via Firebase AI Logic and Local Audio Pipelines**

Dropping STTSFunctions removes the maintenance burden of deploying Node.js or Python Cloud Functions and transcoding audio formats manually4. An inspection of FirebaseExtended/FriendlyMeals-Android and the 2026 Firebase AI Logic updates reveals that every capability previously handled by STTSFunctions—plus advanced agentic grounding—is now supported directly within the client-side **Firebase AI Logic SDK**5.  
Specifically, commits to FriendlyMeals-Android (Add Text-To-Speech via Firebase AI Logic \#12) demonstrate native Gemini Text-to-Speech (TTS) synthesis directly through the Firebase AI Logic SDK without intermediate Cloud Functions5. For interactive multimodal workflows, FriendlyMeals-Android utilizes the liveSession object in Firebase AI Logic to establish a low-latency, bidirectional streaming connection to the **Gemini Live API**16. The Android ViewModel captures microphone audio and throttled camera frames—limiting capture to one frame per second converted to a Bitmap on an I/O coroutine dispatcher to conserve bandwidth and memory—and streams them directly to the session while receiving real-time voice responses and FunctionResponsePart client-side tool triggers16.  
Rather than hardcoding verbose system prompts or model identifiers inside the APK, FriendlyMeals-Android stores prompts in the Firebase Console under AI services \> AI Logic \> Prompt templates and pairs them with **Firebase Remote Config**5. This architecture allows developers to iterate on prompts, adjust daily generation caps, or swap Gemini models instantaneously without redeploying the Android client16. Furthermore, using TemplateTool within Firebase AI Logic enables spatial intelligence via **Grounding with Google Maps**, biasing requests with the user's current latitude, longitude, day of the week, and time to return structured JSON (StoreFinderResult) localized to the user's immediate surroundings40. Because Firebase AI Logic invokes the Gemini Developer API or Vertex AI in Firebase directly from the Android client, pairing SDK initialization with **Firebase App Check** using the **Play Integrity provider** (and DebugAppCheckProvider during emulator or hackathon device testing) is mandatory to attest that traffic originates from an untampered application and prevent billing abuse5. When the device transitions offline, the audio pipeline seamlessly falls back to Android's native on-device SpeechRecognizer and system TextToSpeech, keeping the voice interface operational with zero network dependency.

## **Deep Dive into Architectural Proposals: Offline RAG, System One Routing, and Koog Orchestration**

### **Proposal 1: Constraining Offline Mode to Vector Database Q\&A**

Restricting the offline operational mode of **Gemma 3 270M** strictly to answering questions over personal content stored in the ObjectBox vector database is not merely a pragmatic compromise—it is an architectural necessity for a 270M-parameter model20. While Gemma 3 270M exhibits strong instruction-following capabilities for task-specific workloads relative to its compact size, a 270M parameter weight matrix cannot store reliable open-world parametric knowledge20. If prompted with general knowledge queries offline, an ultra-compact model will inevitably confabulate. However, when the system treats Gemma 3 270M strictly as an extractive synthesis reader over the top\-![][image6] (![][image7]) chunks retrieved from ObjectBox via EmbeddingGemma 2, the task transforms from open-ended recall into local text compression.  
To enforce strict grounding offline, the pipeline should apply a pre-LLM vector distance gate. When ObjectBox executes a nearest-neighbor query via findWithScores(), it returns both the matching MemoryChunkEntity objects and their exact cosine distance scores21. If the nearest neighbor distance exceeds a calibrated relevance threshold, the application short-circuits Gemma 3 270M entirely and immediately returns a deterministic fallback response indicating that no matching information was found in local memory while offline. This mechanism conserves battery, prevents hallucination, and eliminates unnecessary LLM decoding latency. Moreover, because EmbeddingGemma 2 natively embeds images, audio recordings, and video sequences into the exact same 256-dimensional MRL vector space as text19, the offline assistant can also perform zero-LLM multimodal retrieval—matching a natural-language text query directly to an indexed photo or voice note in ObjectBox, mirroring the *Instant Media Search* and *Video Moment Finder* capabilities showcased in the Google AI Edge Gallery8.

### **Proposal 2: Implementing a Jev-Style "System One" Decision Model on the Edge**

Incorporating a **Jev-like "System One" decision model** addresses the single largest latency and reliability bottleneck in edge agent loops: using a slow, autoregressive generative LLM to make routine routing, classification, and tool-safety decisions41. Released by TypeSafe AI in September 2026 (jev-1.13.0), **Jev** is a discriminative transformer model trained on synthetic data via Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), an objective that penalizes miscalibration likely via Brier score loss terms rather than optimizing for human chat preferences (RLHF)41. Instead of generating text token-by-token, Jev takes an unstructured state and evaluates multiple typed questions in parallel in a single pass of 70 to 500 milliseconds, outputting discrete probability distributions and calibrated confidence scores across three multiple-choice primitives: **Choice** (picking from up to 255 categorical options), **Score** (rating an input against ordered levels such as low, medium, and high), and **Noul** (answering a boolean yes-or-no question with a truth probability)41. Because its output conforms to the target schema by construction, Jev achieves a 0.00% structured-output and tool-call error rate, compared to 1.92% and 2.64% error rates across standard frontier LLMs41.  
However, **Jev itself is a proprietary, closed-weight model served exclusively through TypeSafe AI's hosted cloud API** at \$0.042 per million input tokens, with no published weights or on-device runtime41. Consequently, a native LiteRT or MLKit binary of Jev does not exist41.  
![][image8]  
To replicate Jev's **System One** architecture (State ![][image9] \[Choice, Score, Noul\] with calibrated probabilities) locally on Android via LiteRT, the engineering team has two complementary open-weight implementation paths.

#### **Option A: Zero-Marginal-RAM System One Router via EmbeddingGemma 2**

Because **EmbeddingGemma 2 (270M Text)** is already resident in RAM for ObjectBox RAG and natively supports a classification task instruction prefix19, it can double as a discriminative decision engine with zero additional model weight overhead. At application startup, the system pre-computes and caches 256-dimensional embedding centroids ![][image10] for each target route, such as LOCAL\_RAG\_QUERY, DEVICE\_INTENT\_ACTION, LIVE\_CAMERA\_ASSIST, and CLOUD\_ESCALATION. When a user utterance ![][image11] arrives, the router prepends the classification instruction prefix and computes its normalized 256d vector ![][image12] via LiteRT-LM's EmbeddingEngine19. It then evaluates parallel cosine similarities ![][image13] and transforms them into a calibrated probability distribution via a temperature-scaled softmax ![][image14], where temperature ![][image15] is tuned offline using the Brier score to mirror Jev's RLCD calibration19.

#### **Option B: Dedicated LiteRT V2 CompiledModel BERT Intent Classifier**

As independent analyses of Jev observe, its discriminative mechanics closely align with a bidirectional BERT-like encoder architecture44. Empirical studies on Android agent pipelines confirm that a **BERT-based Intent Classifier** running locally outperforms LLM few-shot intent classifiers in routing queries, achieving **0.9171 precision, 0.9691 recall, and 0.9424 F1**, while an accompanying prompt-injection safety classifier achieves **0.9516 precision, 0.9554 recall, and 0.9535 F1**18. Using the **LiteRT V2 CompiledModel API** (com.google.ai.edge.litert:litert:2.2.0), an 8-bit quantized BERT intent classifier .tflite model can be executed with automatic hardware delegate selection and fallback3:

Kotlin  
val options \= CompiledModel.Options().apply {  
    // Attempt NPU acceleration first (Google Tensor / Qualcomm / MediaTek),   
    // then MLDrift GPU, falling back automatically to XNNPACK CPU  
    setAcceleratorPriority(  
        listOf(  
            Accelerator.NPU,  
            Accelerator.GPU,  
            Accelerator.CPU  
        )  
    )  
}  
val systemOneRouter \= CompiledModel.create(context, "system\_one\_bert\_q8.tflite", options)

If a vendor NPU driver fails to compile a specific subgraph, LiteRT V2 automatically isolates the unsupported nodes and routes them to the optimized XNNPACK CPU backend without crashing the application17. Furthermore, by adopting Jev's confidence-gating pattern41, the Android application inspects the maximum output probability ![][image16] to govern execution: high-confidence decisions (![][image17]) trigger local execution automatically, mid-confidence decisions (![][image18]) prompt the user for confirmation before executing sensitive Android Intents, and low-confidence decisions (![][image19]) escalate the query to Firebase AI Logic when online41.

### **Proposal 3: Orchestrating the Hybrid Graph with JetBrains Koog**

Selecting **JetBrains Koog** (ai.koog:koog-agents:1.3.0) as the Android orchestration framework is an exceptional architectural fit that eliminates weeks of custom state-machine plumbing12. While Koog was designed as a Kotlin Multiplatform agent framework, its 2026 release cycle introduced four capabilities tailored directly to hybrid edge-cloud Android applications12.  
First, Koog introduced a dedicated **LiteRTLLMClient** (\#1980) specifically for executing Google's LiteRT models locally on-device, and enhanced it to support **multiple tool calls per response** (\#2073)13. This allows Gemma 3 270M to plug directly into a Koog AIAgent workflow without custom JNI wrapper code12. Second, Koog provides DynamicPromptExecutor and MultiLLMPromptExecutor abstractions that enable an agent to switch LLM providers at any point during a conversation—or reroute dynamically per turn—while adapting and preserving the existing conversation history12. Binding both the local LiteRTLLMClient and the cloud GoogleLLMClient / Firebase AI Logic bridge into a single DynamicPromptExecutor allows the System One router to toggle between offline and online execution transparently12.  
Third, on a 4GB RAM device, allowing Gemma 3 270M's KV-cache to expand across long conversations will spike native memory and degrade token generation speeds. Koog incorporates built-in **intelligent history compression** that summarizes and compresses prior conversational turns to optimize token usage while preserving long-running context12. Fourth, both google-ai-edge/gallery and JetBrains Koog (\#1383, \#2160) have converged on the **Agent Skills specification** (SKILL.md)13. In google-ai-edge/gallery, skills reside in kebab-case directories containing a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter that instructs the local LLM to invoke either run\_intent (to trigger built-in Android OS capabilities such as sending messages or setting alarms) or run\_js (to run custom JavaScript inside a lightweight hidden WebView via window.ai\_edge\_gallery\_get\_result)28. Koog's SkillsDiscovery module natively discovers these skill directories, models them as Skill objects, and generates compact skills-catalog prompts in XML, YAML, or JSON for progressive disclosure—ensuring that a tiny model like Gemma 3 270M is only exposed to full tool parameter schemas when a specific skill is activated13.

| Koog 1.3.0 Capability | Technical Mechanism | Benefit on a 4GB RAM Android Device |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **LiteRTLLMClient (\#1980, \#2073)**13 | Direct Kotlin binding to Google LiteRT local models with multi-tool parsing13 | Eliminates custom C++/JNI LLM orchestration code; supports local function calling13. |
| **DynamicPromptExecutor / MultiLLMPromptExecutor**12 | Runtime resolution and hot-swapping between local and cloud LLMClient instances12 | Routes simple RAG queries to local Gemma 3 270M and complex multimodal tasks to Firebase AI Logic without resetting chat state12. |
| **Intelligent History Compression**12 | Built-in conversation summarization and token pruning12 | Caps Gemma 3 270M KV-cache size under 1K tokens, preventing RAM spikes and lmkd kills12. |
| **Progressive SkillsDiscovery (\#2160)**13 | Generates compact XML/YAML/JSON skill catalogs from SKILL.md directories13 | Prevents prompt bloat on a 270M model by disclosing full tool schemas only upon skill activation13. |
| **Agent Persistence & Fault Tolerance**12 | Checkpoints graph state across execution nodes with automatic retries12 | Restores agent workflow seamlessly if Android's OS lifecycle backgrounds or recreates the Activity12. |

When configuring the Android Gradle build for Koog 1.3.0, engineers must target **JDK 17** or higher and explicitly set **Kotlin 2.3.10** or higher in libs.versions.toml, alongside kotlinx-coroutines 1.10.2, kotlinx-serialization 1.10.0, and kotlinx-datetime 0.7.112. Additionally, because Koog 1.0+ decoupled LLMClient constructors from Ktor in favor of KoogHttpClient.Factory, including ai.koog:koog-agents-additions:1.3.0-beta enables auto-discovery of the HTTP transport on Android, while io.github.oshai:kotlin-logging must be declared explicitly if KLogger is referenced12.

## **End-to-End Execution Flow and Hackathon Implementation Blueprint**

### **Unified Runtime Execution Flow**

At runtime on the 4GB edge device, the rearchitected components operate in a cohesive four-stage loop. During multimodal ingestion and background indexing—modeled on JetPacker's voice note, itinerary, and expense capture workflows6—a background coroutine passes new user notes or media to LiteRT-LM's EmbeddingEngine running embeddinggemma-2-text-270m-litert-lm (or the modular 740m variant when the LLM is idle)19. The engine prepends the title: {title} \| text: {document} prefix, truncates the output vector to 256 dimensions via MRL, normalizes it in float32 or bfloat16, and persists the MemoryChunkEntity into **ObjectBox 5.4.1**22.  
When the user speaks or types a query, the local **System One Router** (either the LiteRT CompiledModel BERT classifier or the EmbeddingGemma 2 classification head) evaluates three typed primitives in parallel within 30 milliseconds: a Noul safety check (is\_safe\_input) to screen out prompt injections from untrusted external text, a Choice routing distribution (intent\_route) over {RAG\_MEMORY\_QA, ANDROID\_NATIVE\_SKILL, LIVE\_CLOUD\_STREAM, GENERAL\_CLOUD\_CHAT}, and a Score rating (complexity\_level) across {LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH}17.  
If the device is offline—or if the System One router selects RAG\_MEMORY\_QA with high confidence and low complexity—**JetBrains Koog** dispatches the request to the local LiteRTLLMClient running **Gemma 3 270M**13. For memory Q\&A, the query is embedded into a 256d vector via EmbeddingGemma 2 and searched against ObjectBox's @HnswIndex22. If the top-3 chunks pass the cosine distance gate, Koog appends them to the prompt via UserPromptAugmenter13 and streams Gemma 3 270M's grounded response to the UI and local TTS. If the router selects ANDROID\_NATIVE\_SKILL, Koog uses SkillsDiscovery to match the request against local SKILL.md definitions and invokes the run\_intent tool to execute the corresponding native Android Intent13.  
Conversely, when the device has network connectivity and the user initiates live camera assistance, requests spatial local search, or triggers a low-confidence score on the local router, Koog's DynamicPromptExecutor routes the turn to **Firebase AI Logic**5. Real-time multimodal sessions open a liveSession stream to the **Gemini Live API** with client-side function calling (FunctionResponsePart) capable of reading and writing directly to the local ObjectBox database, while location-sensitive queries invoke Firebase AI Logic **Server Prompt Templates** with **Google Maps Grounding** (TemplateTool) and synthesize spoken replies via **Gemini TTS**5.

### **Gradle Dependency Specification (build.gradle.kts)**

The following configuration consolidates the exact Maven artifacts required to initialize the Android project:

Kotlin  
// app/build.gradle.kts  
android {  
    namespace \= "com.openmmpa.android"  
    compileSdk \= 35

    defaultConfig {  
        applicationId \= "com.openmmpa.android"  
        minSdk \= 31 // Android 12+ required by Google AI Edge Gallery & LiteRT NPU  
        targetSdk \= 35  
    }  
    compileOptions {  
        sourceCompatibility \= JavaVersion.VERSION\_17 // Required by JetBrains Koog 1.3.0  
        targetCompatibility \= JavaVersion.VERSION\_17  
    }  
}

dependencies {  
    // 1\. JetBrains Koog Agent Orchestrator & LiteRT Client  
    implementation("ai.koog:koog-agents:1.3.0")  
    implementation("ai.koog:koog-agents-additions:1.3.0-beta")  
    implementation("io.github.oshai:kotlin-logging-jvm:7.0.0")

    // 2\. Google AI Edge: LiteRT V2 CompiledModel & LiteRT-LM (Replaces deprecated MediaPipe LLM API)  
    implementation("com.google.ai.edge.litert:litert:2.2.0")  
    implementation("com.google.ai.edge.litert:litert-gpu:2.2.0")  
    implementation("com.google.ai.edge.litert:litert-support:2.2.0")  
    implementation("com.google.ai.edge.litertlm:litertlm-android:0.1.0")

    // 3\. ObjectBox 5.4.1 On-Device HNSW Vector Database  
    implementation("io.objectbox:objectbox-kotlin:5.4.1")  
    implementation("io.objectbox:objectbox-android:5.4.1")

    // 4\. Firebase AI Logic, App Check, & Remote Config (Replaces STTSFunctions)  
    implementation(platform("com.google.firebase:firebase-bom:34.3.0"))  
    implementation("com.google.firebase:firebase-ai") // Firebase AI Logic (Gemini API, Live, TTS, Grounding)  
    implementation("com.google.firebase:firebase-config")  
    implementation("com.google.firebase:firebase-appcheck-playintegrity")  
    debugImplementation("com.google.firebase:firebase-appcheck-debug")  
}

### **Recommended Phased Hackathon Execution Plan**

To maximize development velocity during the hackathon and prevent native memory regressions on the 4GB target device, implementation should follow four sequential milestones:

| Hackathon Phase | Primary Deliverable | Key Technical Validation & Risk Mitigation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Phase 1: Local Vector & Embedding Spine** | ObjectBox 5.4.1 schema (@HnswIndex(dimensions \= 256)) \+ LiteRT-LM EmbeddingEngine with embeddinggemma-2-text-270m-litert-lm19. | Verify MRL truncation to 256d \+ ![][image4] normalization; verify bfloat16/int8 execution (ensuring float16 is disabled so no NaN vectors occur)22. |
| **Phase 2: System One Router & Offline RAG** | Wire **Gemma 3 270M** into Koog's LiteRTLLMClient (1.3.0)12 with the System One router (EmbeddingGemma 2 classification prefix or LiteRT CompiledModel BERT)17. | Enforce the ObjectBox cosine distance gate before invoking Gemma 3 270M; enable Koog history compression to keep total app RAM ![][image20]12. |
| **Phase 3: Agent Skills & Native Intents** | Port 3–4 SKILL.md definitions (run\_intent for alarms, notes, calendar) from google-ai-edge/gallery/skills into Koog's SkillsDiscovery module13. | Validate multi-tool calling in LiteRTLLMClient (\#2073) and progressive XML/JSON catalog disclosure13. |
| **Phase 4: Firebase AI Logic Cloud Augmentation** | Integrate FriendlyMeals-Android patterns: Firebase AI Logic **Gemini TTS**, **Gemini Live API** (liveSession), and **Server Prompt Templates** behind Koog's DynamicPromptExecutor5. | Register the debug secret in **Firebase App Check** (DebugAppCheckProvider)5 and demonstrate seamless airplane-mode switching between Firebase AI Logic and local ObjectBox RAG. |
